\section{Deadlocks in Message-Passing Programs}
\label{sec:deadlocks}

This section provides a brief overview of our developments.
We consider several examples written in FreeST~\cite{freest}, a functional programming language with context-free 
session types.
%~\footnote{The implementation of the proposed 
%solution in FreeST is ongoing work and is out of the scope 
% of this paper.}. 

\subsection{A Classic Deadlock Scenario}
\label{subsec:ex1}
The classic example of a deadlock in message-passing 
programs involves two processes that share two channels. They 
attempt to send in one channel the value received in the other, but do so in an order that prevents synchronization.
Each process holds two linear endpoints, one per channel. 
The two endpoints of the same channel must have \emph
{dual} behavior: if one endpoint sends, the other receives (and vice versa).
In terms of session types, one endpoint should be governed by the type 
\lstinline|T = ?Int; Wait|, which says that the endpoint 
first \emph{receives} an integer and then \emph{waits} to be closed.  
This type showcases the sequential composition operator `\lstinline|;|'.
The other endpoint must then be governed by the type dual to \lstinline|T|, which first \emph{sends} an integer and then \emph{closes} the channel (denoted \lstinline|!Int; Close|).
%Dually, the other 
%endpoint must then first \emph{receive} 
%an integer and then \emph{wait} to 
%be closed, which is denoted as `$\tseq{?{\tint}}{\twait{ }}$'. 

In FreeST~\cite{freest}, each process can be implemented  as follows:
\begin{lstlisting}
type T = ?Int; Wait

f : T -> dualof T 1-> ()
f x y =
  let (n,x) = receive x in
  let y = send n y in
  wait x;
  close y
\end{lstlisting}

The two arguments of \lstinline|f|  (\lstinline|x| and \lstinline|y|) 
represent endpoints of two distinct channels. 
Their types are, respectively, \lstinline|T| and \lstinline|dualof T|,  which implicitly denotes  \lstinline|!Int; Close|.
Notice that the second arrow represents a \emph{linear} function (denoted by \lstinline|1->|) which must be used \emph{once}, since its context contains a linear channel (of type \lstinline|T|).

% we use both the usual arrow type \lstinline|->| and the \emph{linear} arrow type \lstinline|1->|.

In functional implementations of sessions, such as FreeST, functions operate on endpoints and consume them gradually according to their protocol. 
This way, given an endpoint \lstinline|x|, the function \lstinline|receive x| returns a pair: the received value and an endpoint (the continuation of \lstinline|x|); similarly, given a value \lstinline|v| and an endpoint \lstinline|y|, the function \lstinline|send v y| returns the continuation of \lstinline|y|.
Also, \lstinline|wait x| and \lstinline|close y| are explicit mechanisms for closing a channel. With these intuitions in place, we see that \lstinline|f|
 proceeds as prescribed by its type: it receives on 
\lstinline|x|, sends on \lstinline|y|, and then closes both channels.


Consider now the following function \lstinline|main|, which first uses the \lstinline|new| operation to  create fresh identifiers for the endpoints, and then launches two processes in parallel, each of them running an instance of function \lstinline|f| (with appropriate parameters in each case):

\lstset{firstnumber=9}
\begin{lstlisting}
main : ()
main =
  let (r1, w1)  = new @T () in
  let (r2, w2)  = new @T () in
  fork (\_:() 1-> f r1 w2);
  f r2 w1
\end{lstlisting}
\lstset{firstnumber=1}

Note that this program type-checks: the 
behavior of the channels (receiving/sending an integer and closing)
is locally respected. 
Now, it is not difficult to see that the resulting program enters into a \emph{deadlock}:
both processes are blocked, waiting to 
receive on both channels, and neither is enabled to send the value to be 
received. 

\paragraph{Addressing deadlocks using priorities.}
To avoid getting blocked at run-time, one solution is to enrich the 
types so as to enable a more informed \emph{static analysis} of 
the order of operations in the program body. Following 
Padovani and Novara~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364, DBLP:conf/forte/PadovaniN15}, we annotate the types with the \emph{priorities} associated to the corresponding 
operation. 
(Throughout the document we highlight the new additions to 
the type system---the priorities---with colour \textcolor{teal}{teal}.)

Revisiting our classic deadlock scenario, 
the types that govern the two channels  should now be typed
differently, priority-wise: 
%
\begin{lstlisting}
type R = ?~p~Int; Wait ~(p+2)~
type S = ?~q~Int; Wait ~(q+2)~
\end{lstlisting}
%
Type \lstinline|R| extends \lstinline|T| with priorities: it receives an \lstinline|Int| at priority \lstinline|~p~|
and then waits at priority \lstinline|~p+2~|, while 
type \lstinline|S| is similar: it extends  \lstinline|T| under priority 
\lstinline|~q~|.
To showcase the use of priorities, consider a variant of  \lstinline|main| that launches the two functions  \lstinline|f| and  \lstinline|g|:

\lstset{firstnumber=3}

\begin{lstlisting}
f : R ->~[top, bot]~ dualof S 1->~[p, q+2]~ ()
f x y =
  let (n,x) = receive x in -- priority: p
  let y = send n y in      -- priority: q
  wait x;                  -- priority: p+2
  close y                  -- priority: q+2

g : S ->~[top, bot]~ dualof R 1->~[q, p+2]~ ()
g y x =
  let (n,y) = receive y in -- priority: q
  let x = send n x in      -- priority: p
  wait y;                  -- priority: q+2
  close x                  -- priority: p+2
\end{lstlisting}

Following Padovani and Novara~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364,DBLP:conf/forte/PadovaniN15},
we use priority annotations on arrow types: they provide \emph{boundaries} for the input/output behavior of a function.
The annotations in the first arrow of \lstinline|f| mean that 
there is no 
channel in the function environment (represented by 
\lstinline|~top~|) and that there is no \emph{latent effect} after
function application (represented by \lstinline|~bot~|); for 
the second arrow, \lstinline|x| is already in the 
environment (represented with priority \lstinline|~p~| in the 
annotation) and after  application we expect 
to have operations up to priority \lstinline|~q+2~|.
The annotations for the arrows in the type of \lstinline|g| are analogous.

We can now follow each function by considering the involved priorities; we detail them on the right of each instruction. 
We realize that we have a mismatch:
according to the order of operations (and the typing rules
presented in \Cref{sec:semantics}), function \lstinline|f| 
requires \lstinline|~p~| < \lstinline|~q~| (Lines 3 and 4)
whereas function \lstinline|g| requires \lstinline|~q~| < \lstinline|~p~| (Lines 10 and~11). 
This mismatch is detected during type checking, when the (updated) \lstinline|main| function launches \lstinline|f| and \lstinline|g| in parallel threads.
There are no \lstinline|~p~| and \lstinline|~q~| that satisfy both requirements, which is sufficient grounds to statically identify a deadlock.
The programmer must then refactor their program 
to ensure that the order of operations meets the corresponding 
priorities. In this case, it suffices to swap the operations
receive/send and wait/close in one of the functions.



\subsection{Deadlocks and Simple Recursion}

Session types naturally take advantage of recursion and are 
usually equi-recursive. As Padovani and Novara 
observe~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364}, recursion introduces its 
challenges, which are actually very familiar to issues found in the theory of context-free 
session types~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/ThiemannV16}.

Consider a (session) type \lstinline|Stream| that sends an 
infinite sequence of unit values. This may be specified as 
$\trec{\svar}{\tseq{!\tunit }{\svar}}$, where $\svar$ denotes a recursive variable. We could  write a program for two communicating \lstinline|Stream|s as 
follows (noting that \lstinline|()| represents the $\tunit$ 
type in FreeST):

\lstset{firstnumber=1}

\begin{lstlisting}
type Stream1 = !~p~() ; Stream1
type Stream2 = !~q~() ; Stream2
  
client : Stream1 ->~[top,bot]~ dualof Stream2 
                1->~[p,q]~ ()
client c1 c2 =
  let c1 = send () c1 in      -- priority: p
  let (_,c2) = receive c2 in  -- priority: q
  client c1 c2
\end{lstlisting}

With an ``appropriate'' communicating \lstinline|server|, 
the program above could successfully pass the type check. 
However, due to the equirecursive nature of our types, 
nothing prevents us from anticipating that the client will 
do more than one pair send/receive message and trying to write 
the following (behaviourally equivalent) program:

\lstset{firstnumber=10}
\begin{lstlisting}    
client' : Stream1 ->~[top,bot]~ dualof Stream2 
                 1->~[p,q]~ ()
client' c1 c2 =
  -- first send/receive
  let c1 = send () c1 in     --priority: p
  let (_,c2) = receive c2 in --priority: q
  -- second send/receive
  let c1 = send () c1 in     --priority: p (!)
  let (_,c2) = receive c2 in --priority: q (!)
  client' c1 c2
\end{lstlisting}

In Lines 7 and 8, we see that equi-recursion re-introduces 
priorities that make the program ill-typed. Revisiting the 
thorough analysis by Thiemann et 
al.~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/ThiemannV16,DBLP:journals/iandc/AlmeidaMTV22}, we realize that
the need to enable \emph{polymorphic recursion} is now 
apparent at the level of priorities. To that end, we 
propose \emph{priority abstraction} to allow the type to evolve 
without entering an inconsistent state.
Along the lines of type abstraction, we use a quantifier
$\fforall\,\prvar^{\intervalvar}$ to abstract over priorities 
and bind a \emph{priority
variable} $\prvar$ to a \emph{priority interval} $\intervalvar$, as 
proposed by Padovani 
and Novara~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364}.
Using priority abstraction, the type \lstinline|Stream| can then be defined by:
\[\trec{\svar}{(\tpolyp{\pr}{\intervaloo{\bot}{\top}}{\tseq{\tout{\tunit}{\pr}}{\svar}}))}.\] 
A channel of this type starts by instantiating the 
priority variable $\priority{\pr}$ 
with an integer that materializes the order/urgency of 
the send operation; such an integer should lay in the interval 
$\intervaloo{\prbot}{\prtop}$. Then, it sends a unit value and finally recurs and 
starts all over again.

%\end{document}

Our \lstinline|client'| function can now be (correctly) defined as:

\lstset{firstnumber=1}
\begin{lstlisting}
type Stream = ~forallp i belongsTo (bot,top) =>~ !~i~() ; Stream
  
client' : ~forallp p,q belongsTo (bot,top) => ~Stream ->~[top,bot]~ dualof Stream 1->~[p,q+2]~ ()
client' c1 c2 =      -- c1 : Stream
                     -- c2 : Stream
  -- first send/receive
  let c1 = send () c1~{p}~ in     -- priority: p
                                -- c1 : Stream  
  let (_,c2) = receive c2~{q}~ in -- priority: q
  -- second send/receive        -- c2 : Stream
  let c1 = send () c1~{p+2}~ in   --priority:p+2    
                                -- c1 : Stream 
  let (_, c2) = receive c2~{q+2}~ in -- pr.: q+2
                                -- c2 : Stream   
  client'~{p+4}{q+4}~ c1 c2
\end{lstlisting}

In Line 7, we instantiate the priority variable of  
\lstinline|c1| with value \lstinline|~p~|, send the
unit value in \lstinline|c1|, then receive in \lstinline|c2|
instantiated with priority \lstinline|~q~| and then repeat 
these operations, instantiated with \lstinline|~p+2~| and 
\lstinline|~q+2~|, respectively. Our typing rules
(\Cref{sec:semantics}) will require 
\lstinline|~p~| < \lstinline|~q~| < \lstinline|~p+2~| < \lstinline|~q+2~|, which should be satisfiable.
Finally, the recursive function call is instantiated with 
the next priorities: \lstinline|~p+4~| and \lstinline|~q+4~|. 

\subsection{Deadlocks and Non-Regular Recursion}
\label{ss:trees}
Context-free session types shine with \emph{non-regular recursion}. 
The classic example that capitalises on all the features of 
context-free session types is exchanging binary 
trees~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/ThiemannV16,DBLP:conf/tacas/AlmeidaMV20}.
Consider the type \lstinline|TreeChannel| given by:
\[\trec{\svar}{(\tpolyp{\pr}{\intervaloo{\bot}{\top}}{\&^{\priority{\pr}}\{\keyword{LeafC}: \tskip, \keyword{NodeC}: \tseq{\tin{\tint}{\pr+1}}{\tseq{\svar}{\svar}}\}{}}{})}.\]
A channel governed by this type starts by 
instantiating the priority variable $\priority{\pr}$
and then offers two branches:  one with label 
$\keyword{LeafC}$ that proceeds by doing nothing (represented 
by type $\tskip$), and another 
with label $\keyword{NodeC}$, that receives an integer 
under priority $\priority{\pr+1}$ and then receives the 
left subtree followed by the right subtree.  

Consider the implementation of function \lstinline|receiveTree| under 
our priority-based approach to deadlock-freedom:
%\todo{Jorge, please check all the annotations in the arrows of the examples, please}

\begin{lstlisting}
data Tree = Leaf | Node Int Tree Tree

type TreeChannel = ~forallp p belongsTo (bot,top) => ~
  &~p~{LeafC: Skip, 
     NodeC: ?~(p+1)~Int;TreeChannel;TreeChannel}

receiveTree : ~forallp p belongsTo (bot,top) => ~
          TreeChannel; a ->~[top,p+1]~ (Tree, a)
receiveTree c =
  match c~{p}~ with {
    LeafC c ->
     (Leaf, c),
    NodeC c ->
     let (x, c) = receive c in
     let (left, c) = receiveTree~{p+2}~ @(TreeChannel ; a) c in
     let (right, c) = receiveTree~{p+4}~ @a c in
     (Node x left right, c)
  }
\end{lstlisting}

The signature of \lstinline|receiveTree| states
that the function holds under some priority \lstinline|~p~| and
receives a channel of type \lstinline|TreeChannel; a|, where 
\lstinline|a| is a \emph{type variable}. (FreeST implicitly binds 
all type variables occurring free in a function signature.)
This type variable is instantiated in a function call 
through the \lstinline|@| operator (Lines 15 and 16).
Finally, it should return a pair with a reconstruction of the
\lstinline|Tree| and the continuation of the input channel. 
The function \lstinline|match| handles the 
choices on \lstinline|c|, instantiated with priority
\lstinline|~p~|: for \lstinline|LeafC| it 
returns a pair with a \lstinline|Leaf| and the 
continuation of the channel; for \lstinline|NodeC|, the 
function  receives the integer on channel
\lstinline|c| and then receives the left and right subtrees. 

Notice that the recursive calls apply polymorphic recursion 
on both types and priorities: in the first call (Line 15), 
the  {priority variable} needs to be 
instantiated with the updated priority \lstinline|~p+2~| and 
the  {type variable} is updated with the 
type of the continuation of the channel 
(\lstinline|TreeChannel;a|). In the second call the 
priorities need to account for the latent effect in the 
function application in line 15 and the reminder of the 
channel has now type \lstinline|a|. Finally, the function
returns a pair composed of the reconstruction of the node
followed by the continuation of the channel. 

Lines 15 and 16 illustrate the harmonious way in which our 
context-free session types integrate priorities: the 
programmers are already used to reason about the 
instantiation channels at each recursive 
call~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/ThiemannV16,DBLP:conf/tacas/AlmeidaMV20}. 
With negligible overhead they do this reasoning
at the level of priorities.

\subsection{Polymorphic Recursion over Priorities}
\label{subsec:shift-mismatch}

By abstracting over priorities and handling priorities and 
types seamlessly, we gain expressive power when compared 
to Padovani and Novara's \emph{displacements}~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364}, which shift 
priorities in recursive calls. Displacements have 
some limitations, as acknowledged by the 
authors. Indeed, they identify 
a \emph{non-regular} pattern of the \lstinline|filterStream|
function, which forwards values received depending on whether 
the filter validates the values or not. This introduces
an asymmetry on the number of  {unfolds} of the 
\emph{sender stream} when compared to the 
\emph{receiver stream}. As we are able to tune the 
instantiation of priorities in each function call, we can 
now correctly implement and validate such function:

\begin{lstlisting}
type InputStream = ~forallp p belongsTo (bot,top) => ~
                   ?~p~ Int; InputStream

filterStream : ~forallp p belongsTo (bot,top), q belongsTo (p,top) => ~
    (Int ->~[top,bot]~ Bool) 
                  ->~[top,bot]~ InputStream
                  ->~[top,bot]~ dualof InputStream 
                 1->~[p,q+1]~ ()
filterStream f x y = 
  let (v, x) = receive x~{p}~ in -- priority : p
  if (f v) then 
    let y = send v y~{q}~ in     -- priority : q
    filterStream~{p+1}{q+1}~ f x y  
  else 
    filterStream~{p+1}{q+1}~ f x y
\end{lstlisting}

Our approach is able to correctly type cases that do not 
folow a ``regular 
pattern''. Indeed, context-free session types traditionally 
handle \emph{non-regular} patterns, after all.

Having illustrated our type systems via examples, we now formally introduce it and establish its properties.

\section{Context-Free Session Types, with Priorities}
\label{sec:types}

Types are split into two different syntactic categories:
functional types and session types.
%
The syntax of types relies on some base sets: 
$\ell\in L$ stands for labels, $\tvar$ stands for

As we have seen, $\priority{\pr}$, $\prvar$, and $\priority{\intervalvar}$ stand for priorities, priority variables, and priority intervals, respectively.
We use $\prbot$ and $\prtop$ to stand for the lowest and highest 
priority, respectively.

Notice that by considering two syntactic categories 
we avoid the need for a kinding system~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/ThiemannV16,DBLP:journals/iandc/AlmeidaMTV22}, but
entails some duplication: polymorphic types can 
either have a \emph{functional} body, in which case the 
quantifier binds a 
\emph{functional} type variable, or the body can be a session, 
in which case the quantifier binds a \emph{session} type 
variable; the same for recursive types. This means that in addition 
to $\tvar\neq \svar$, we also have two different (but overloaded)
$\forall$ and $\mu$ operators. 
Recursive 
types keep their body's original ``nature'', whereas polymorphic
types are always functional. (We leave the details of this 
choice to previous work on context-free session 
types~\cite{DBLP:conf/tacas/AlmeidaMV20}.)

%  Traditionally, the 
% well-formedness of context-free session types is accompained by a kinding 
% system~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/ThiemannV16,DBLP:conf/tacas/AlmeidaMV20}. 
% To simplify the notation, we consider two different 
% syntactic categories of types. This choice requires
% some redundancy,  

As discussed in \Cref{sec:deadlocks}, the distinguishing feature of our proposal is the 
incorporation of priority 
annotations~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364,DBLP:conf/forte/PadovaniN15,DBLP:journals/lmcs/KokkeD23} in 
context-free session 
types~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/ThiemannV16}.
The function type 
$\tarrow{T}{U}{\pr_1}{\pr_2}{m}$ is decorated with a 
\emph{lower priority bound} $\priority{\pr_1}$ indicating that the closure of 
the function contains channels with priority $\priority{\pr_1}$ or 
greater, and an \emph{upper priority bound} $\priority{\pr_2}$ standing for 
the maximum priority that is pending in the function and 
will be triggered once the function is applied (see the comprehensive 
explanation by 
Padovani and Novara~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364} for further details). 
The multiplicity $m$ determines how many times the function can be used:
$\linmult$ means that it can be used once, 
$\unmult$ means that the function can be used zero or 
more times. 
% We often omit the annotations when functions are \emph{pure}: $\rightarrow_m^{\prtop, \prbot}$.

In polymorphic types ($\tpolyt{\alpha}{\pr}{T}{\prsigma}, 
\tpolyt{\svar}{\pr}{S}{\prsigma}$), the type variable is assigned to a 
priority $\pr$. Priorities are  
defined in terms of priority variables $\prvar$, that are
abstracted through a $\fforall$ binder that assigns to $\prvar$ a 
priority interval $\priority{\intervalvar}$. Following prior works~\cite{DBLP:conf/fossacs/Padovani14,DBLP:journals/lmcs/KokkeD23,padovani:hal-00954364}, 
the exchange of messages (send/receive, internal/external choice) and close/wait operate under a priority $\pr$. Type $\tskip$ and sequential composition 
do not explicitly represent an operation, so do not require any priority annotation.
We denote the set of \emph{free 
type variables} in a type $T$ as $\ftv{T}$ and the set of \emph{free priority variables} as $\fpv{T}$.



\cref{fig:priorities} gives the syntax of priorities and 
priority intervals, which follows Padovani and Novara's work~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364}. Types with priority $\prtop$ correspond to  
so-called \emph{unrestricted types}~\cite{vasconcelos2012fundamentals}. 
Priorities can also be integer values $\priority{n}$, 
priority variables $\prvar$, the maximum or minimum 
of two priorities ($\prglb{\pr}{\prsigma}$ and 
$\prlub{\pr}{\prsigma}$, respectively) or 
a \emph{displacement} $\prdisp{\pr}{\prsigma}$, 
representing the addition of integers extended with the
following rules $\prdisp{\pr}{\prbot} = \prbot$ and 
$\prdisp{\pr}{\prtop} = \prtop$. Priority intervals can 
either be closed or open to account for the inclusion of 
the limits.

\paragraph{Type formation}

Not all types are well formed. For example, we do not want 
type $\tout{(\tout{\tint}{1})}{2}$ to be well-formed since 
the operation that follows in the payload is \emph{more urgent}, 
i.e., has lower priority, than sending the message itself. 
We also do not wish to define the type 
$\tpolyt{\tvar}{\prvar}{\tin{\tvar}{\pr}}{}$ if $\prvar$ and $\pr$
are not properly defined.

Paving our way to type formation, typing contexts for
polymorphic and priority variables are 
presented in~\cref{fig:typing-ctx-poly}. We record  
polymorphic variables
with the corresponding priority assignment in environment 
$\envpoly$ and priority variables with the respective 
range in environment $\envpr$. 



To properly control the order of operations, we  often need to refer to the priority of a type. 
Given a type $T$, its priority $\lowestpriorityEnv{T}$ is defined as the lowest priority of its 
operations---see~\cref{fig:priority-types}.
Note in particular that $\lowestpriorityEnv{\tskip}=\prtop$ and that the priority of 
$\tseq{S_1}{S_2}$ follows that of ${S_1}$.
Our comparison relations should be considered 
up to the assignments in $\envpr$~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364}, 
which will be denoted with a subscript~$\envpr$.
For instance: for $\envpr_0 = \{ \priority{\prvar_1} \in \intervaloo{\prbot}{\prtop},
\priority{\prvar_2} \in \intervalco{\prbot}{\prvar_1}, \priority{\prvar_3} \in 
\intervaloc{\prvar_1}{\prtop}\}$, the relations 
$\priority{\prvar_2} <_{\envpr_0} \priority{\prvar_1}$ and 
$\priority{\prvar_1} <_{\envpr_0} \priority{\prvar_3}$ hold.

The judgement  $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr}{T}$ 
denotes that type $T$ is well-formed under the polymorphic context $\envpoly$
and the priority context $\envpr$. The rules for type formation are 
defined in~\cref{fig:type-formation}. The type formation rules 
\textsf{F-Unit}, \textsf{F-Abs}, \textsf{F-Pair}, \textsf{F-Close}, \textsf{F-Wait}, 
\textsf{F-Skip} and \textsf{F-Var} are standard.
Rule \textsf{F-MsgOut} (resp., \textsf{F-MsgIn}) requires that the priority 
of the send (resp., receive) operation is lower than the priority of the payload.
Rules \textsf{F-IntChoice} and \textsf{F-ExtChoice} require the 
choice operation to be \emph{more urgent} than the continuation types.

Rule \textsf{F-TAbs} states that a polymorphic type $\tpolyt{\gamma}{\pr}{T}{}$ 
can only assign a type variable $\gamma$
to a priority variable $\pr$ if all the free priority variables occurring
in $\pr$ are defined in $\envpr$; furthermore, $T$ should be well-typed
under the extended environment $\envpoly, \gamma::\pr$.
Similarly, rule \textsf{F-PAbs} states that a priority variable $\prvar$
can only be assigned to $\intervalvar$ through the $\fforall$ binder
if all the free priority variables occurring in $\intervalvar$ are defined 
in $\envpr$; furthermore, the body of the type should be well-typed 
under the priority environment $\envpr, \prvar\in \intervalvar$.

Rule \textsf{F-Rec} states that a recursive type $\trec{\gamma}{T}$ is 
well-typed if $T$ is well-typed under the extended context $\envpoly, \gamma :: \pr$
and $T$ is contractive, meaning that $T$ should have no subterms 
of the form $\mu \alpha. \mu \alpha_1. \ldots \mu \alpha_n . \alpha$, considering 
an adaption of the conventional notion of 
contractivity~\cite{DBLP:journals/acta/GayH05} to account 
for $\tskip$ as the neutral element of the sequential composition. (A rule-based 
definition of contractivity can be found in previous 
works~\cite{DBLP:conf/tacas/AlmeidaMV20,DBLP:conf/concur/SilvaMV23}.)

Finally, Rule \textsf{F-Seq} states that a sequential composition $\tseq{T_1}{T_2}$
is well-formed if both $T_1$ and $T_2$ are. It may seem
natural to impose the restriction 
$\lowestpriorityEnv{T_1} <_\envpr \lowestpriorityEnv{T_2}$, but this would 
invalidate the monoidal properties of context-free session types, namely that
$\tskip$ is the neutral element of sequential composition and can, therefore, 
be used without jeopardising the well-formedness of types. For example, the 
type  $\tseq{\tout{\tint}{1}}{\tseq{\tskip}{\tin{\tunit}{2}}}$ can be used  
where the type $\tseq{\tout{\tint}{1}}{\tin{\tunit}{2}}$ is expected (see the typing rule \textsf{T-Eq}). Note that, by its nature, 
$\tskip$ is an \emph{invisible type}, i.e., it does not exhibit behaviour and 
is uninhabited. This means that we will be able to impose this natural
\emph{priority ordering} at 
the level of the typing rules (\cref{sec:semantics}). 

\paragraph{Type duality}

Duality is paramount to establish \emph{compatible} communication 
between two endpoints of a channel. This notion is defined only 
over session types and is presented in~\cref{fig:duality}.
The definition is 
standard~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/ThiemannV16,DBLP:conf/tacas/AlmeidaMV20}. Since we are dealing with higher-order sessions,
in the sense that channels can be conveyed into messages, 
the duality of recursive types relies on  
\emph{negative references}, which serve to dualize 
recursive sessions properly~\cite{jlamp}. 
Duality preserves priorities: 
for that reason, the dual of a priority abstraction 
($\dualof{\tpolyp{\svar}{\pr}{S}{\prsigma}}$)
is the priority abstraction 
of the dual session type: $\tpolyp{\svar}{\pr}{\dualof{S}}{\prsigma}$. 



\begin{figure}

    \dualof{\tskip} &= \tskip
    &
    \dualof{\tseq{S_1}{S_2}} &= \tseq{\dualof{S_1}}{\dualof{S_2}}\\
    \dualof{\tout{T}{\pr}} &= \tin{T}{\pr} 
    &
    \dualof{\tclose{\pr}} &= \twait{\pr} \\
    \dualof{\tin{T}{\pr}} &= \tout{T}{\pr}
    &

    \dualof{\tintchoice{\ell}{S_\ell}{\ell\in L}{\pr}} &= \textchoice{\ell}{\dualof{S_\ell}}{\ell\in L}{\pr}

    \dualof{\textchoice{\ell}{S_\ell}{\ell\in L}{\pr}} &= \tintchoice{\ell}{\dualof{S_\ell}}{\ell\in L}{\pr}
    &
    \dualof{\tpolyp{\svar}{\pr}{S}{\prsigma}} &= \enspace \tpolyp{\svar}{\pr}{\dualof{S}}{\prsigma}

\end{figure}

Our term language is a call-by-value concurrent language that  extends earlier proposals for context-free
session types~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/ThiemannV16,DBLP:conf/tacas/AlmeidaMV20}, 
incorporating applications and abstractions over priority 
variables. 

\cref{fig:terms} presents the syntax of constants, values, expressions and configurations. 
As customary in functional languages with sessions (cf.~\cite{DBLP:journals/jfp/GayV10}), session communication is defined at the level of \emph{configurations}, which is where deadlocks could occur.
Formally, a configuration is either an expression, 
a parallel composition of configurations, or a configuration in the scope of a channel restriction $\confnu{x}{y}{-}$ that binds together the endpoints $x$ and $y$. 
Differently from prior works on context-free session types, here we consider
\emph{flagged} configurations, which indicate whether the configuration is the main thread ($\phi = \mainthread$) or is a child thread ($\phi= \childthread$). 

Further novelties concern priorities and their associated constructs.
Priority abstractions are of the form $\eprabs{\prvar}{e}$, where
$\mathbb{\Lambda}$ bounds a priority variable $\prvar$ that might occur free
in $e$. Like type abstractions, priority abstractions of the form 
$\eprabs{\prvar}{v}$ are values. Priority applications over 
an expression $e$ are denoted by $\eprapp{e}{\pr}$. 
There are several forms of partial 
applications for constants, which are considered values; they will be justified by 
the types presented in~\cref{fig:types-constants}. 
We denote by $\fv{\e}$ the set of free (term) variables occurring in $\e$.

\cref{fig:types-constants} defines types for constants. By upgrading 
priorities to the level of types, we can give proper types to all constants 
instead of relying on type schemes, as in~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364,DBLP:journals/lmcs/KokkeD23}.
Following Padovani and Novara's proposal~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364}, 
our priority binders control the order of operations  
in a type. We discuss these types:
\begin{itemize}
	\item 
The constant $\efork$ receives a thunk with whatever
priority $\priority{\prvar_1}$ and latent effect $\priority{\prvar_2}$, returns 
$\eunit$ and has no latent effect (signalled with $\prbot$ as the second 
annotation of the arrow). 
\item The type of $\esend$ starts by binding the priority 
$\priority{\prvar_1}$ of the payload, then requires the priority of the 
send operation to be lower (i.e., more urgent) than that of the payload 
and, finally, the lowest priority of the continuation channel should be 
higher than that of the send operation. After all type and priority variables are instantiated, function $\esend$ expects an 
input value to be sent, then expects an input channel of type 
$\tseq{\tout{\tvar}{\prvar_2}}{\svar}$ and returns the continuation channel 
$\svar$. It has latent effect $\priority{\prvar_2}$, meaning that as soon 
as function $\esend$ is fully applied, it triggers operations with 
priority at most $\priority{\prvar_2}$. 
\item The interpretation of the types for $\ereceive$,
$\eclose$ and $\ewait$ is similar to that of $\esend$. 
\item The type of $\efix$ is standard; the 
recursive functions presented in the examples use the $\efix$ point 
operator implicitly.
\end{itemize}

Having seen the types for constants, the different value shapes in~\cref{fig:terms} 
become clearer. If we let ourselves be guided by the type of $\esend$, we 
realize that we can apply it to a priority and get a partial application 
$\eprapp{\esend}{\pr}$, or further make a type application and get 
$\etapp{\eprapp{\esend}{\pr}}{T}$. Then, we can choose to do one or two 
priority applications again, reaching $\eprapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\esend}{\pr}}{T}}{\prsigma}$ 
and $\eprapp{\eprapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\esend}{\pr}}{T}}{\prsigma}}{\prpi}$. At 
this point, we are left with another type application yielding the value 
$\etapp{\eprapp{\eprapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\esend}{\pr}}{T}}{\prsigma}}{\prpi}}{S}$ 
which has type $\tarrow{\tarrow{T}{\tseq{\tout{T}{\prsigma}}{S}}{\prtop}{\prbot}{\unmult}}{S}{\top}{\prsigma}{\linmult}$. 
Before we get $\esend$ fully applied, we can do a term-level application of the 
previous expression to a value $v$ and get the expression 
$\eapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\eprapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\esend}{\pr}}{T}}{\prsigma}}{\prpi}}{S}}{v}$, 
which is still considered a value.
For the other constants, the reasoning is similar.

The typing judgement $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{e}{T}{\rho}$ means
that an expression $e$ has type $T$ and an upper bound $\priority{\rho}$ 
on its priority under the typing environments $\envpoly, \envtvars$
and $\envpr$. 

\cref{fig:typing-rules-expr} presents our typing rules, which 
result from incorporating the priority-based approach to 
deadlock-freedom~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364, DBLP:conf/forte/PadovaniN15, DBLP:journals/lmcs/KokkeD23}
in the type system of context-free session types~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/ThiemannV16,DBLP:conf/tacas/AlmeidaMV20}. 

We comment on the typing rules. 
Constants are 
typed through \textsf{T-Const} according to the types 
assigned in~\cref{fig:types-constants}; they have no 
effect ($\prbot$) and assume that the typing context 
$\envtvars$ has priority $\prtop$, i.e., it is 
\emph{unrestricted}. Rule \textsf{T-Var} also requires 
that variables are typed under an unrestricted environment, 
with no effect. 

We have three forms of abstraction (on types, priorities, and terms).
Rule \textsf{T-TAbs} states that a type 
abstraction $\etabs{\tvar}{\e}$ has type $\tpolyt{\tvar}{\pr}{T}{}$ with no effect if $\e$ has type $T$ under the extended 
polymorphic environment $\envpoly, \tvar :: \pr$, assuming 
that the free priority variables occurring in $\pr$ are 
defined in $\envpr$ and that the typing environment $\envtvars$ is 
unrestricted---because we do not want to abstract over linear values. 
Rule \textsf{T-PAbs} is similar with the expected adaption to priority abstractions.
Rules \textsf{T-AbsLin} and \textsf{T-AbsUn} consider linear and unrestricted functions, respectively; in the latter case, the context $\envtvars$ should be unrestricted. 
In terms of priorities, both rules
state that the 
lower priority bound coincides with the lowest 
priority in the typing context $\envtvars$ and the upper
priority bound is the effect of evaluating the body of 
the function. 

Rule \textsf{T-TApp} is standard with the 
extra proviso that $\lowestpriorityEnv{T}$ coincides with 
$\pr$ under the priority context $\envpr$. 
Rule \textsf{T-PApp} is new 
and states that a priority $\pr$ can instantiate 
$\prvar$ if $\pr$ belongs to the priority interval assigned to 
$\prvar$;  all the occurrences of $\prvar$ in $U$
are updated with the new value $\pr$. Rule \textsf{T-App} is standard 
for \emph{call-by-value} evaluation strategies~\cite
{padovani:hal-00954364}: it requires the first expression to have a 
\emph{more urgent} priority than the typing context for the second 
expression and the effect of the second expression to be \emph{more 
urgent} than the priority of the type of the first expression (that is, by then, 
reduced to a value). Rule \textsf{T-Pair} follows a similar reasoning. 

Rule \textsf{T-LetPair} has a proviso stating that the effect of $e_1$ 
is lower than the lowest priority of the typing environment for $\e_2$. 
\textsf{T-LetUnit} requires that the channels used for evaluating 
$\e_1$ have lowest priority than those occurring in $\e_2$. 
This constraint enforces an increasing order of priorities between successive operations, thus complementing the omission of an analogous constraint in rule \textsf{F-Seq}, as observed in~\cref{sec:types}.

Rule 
\textsf{T-Sel} assigns no effect ($\prbot$) to the evaluation of 
$\eselect{k}$, requires the priority of the choice operation to be 
lower than that of the continuation types and also that the typing 
environment has no channel left, i.e., has priority $\prtop$. Rule 
\textsf{T-Match} treats $\e_\ell$ as if it were a function (see \textsf
{T-AbsLin}) and, according to the call-by-value evaluation strategy, 
requires the evaluation of $\e$ to be more urgent than that of 
$\e_\ell$. 

Rule \textsf{T-Eq} states that an 
expression that is well typed against a type is well typed against any 
of its equivalent types. Type equivalence has been the subject of much 
development for context-free session types~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/ThiemannV16,DBLP:journals/iandc/AlmeidaMTV22,costa2022higher,almeida2020deciding}. 
The judgement of type equivalence used in rule \textsf{T-Eq} is the 
trivial extension of previous proposals by considering only the comparison 
of types and type constructors with exactly the same priority.

Finally, \textsf{T-New} requires the typing 
environment to be un\-re\-strict\-ed and type $S$ to be well-formed and \emph{not equivalent} 
to $\tskip$, to ensure that there are some pending operations. We could have  
considered $\keyword{new}$ as a constant; this would require  
priorities to be instantiated at the type level and 
channels to be created with types already \emph{committed} to a priority.

\cref{fig:typing-rules-proc} presents the typing rules for configurations. 
Rules \textsf{C-Child} and \textsf{C-Main} distinguish the typing of child and main threads: 
while any expression (closed for priority and polymorphic variables)

and \textsf{C-New} are standard: the former splits the context and 
considers the greatest flag for the typing judgement, and the latter introduces two dual 
endpoints of a channel in the typing context.

\section{Dynamics: Type Preservation and Deadlock Freedom} 
\label{sec:safety}
\paragraph{Operational semantics.}
\cref{fig:reduction} presents the expression and 
configuration reduction rules considering a call-by-value evaluation 
strategy. Evaluation 
contexts also reflect the left-to-right evaluation strategy and 
are defined by the grammar at the top of~\cref{fig:reduction}. 
The expression reduction rules are standard for a call-by-value 
lambda calculus, except that we have  added a new $\beta$-reduction rule for 
priority-level abstractions (\textsf{E-PApp}). 

Configuration reduction includes
rules to lift reductions from expressions to configurations 
(\textsf{R-LiftE}) and from configurations to configuration contexts
(\textsf{R-LiftC}). \textsf{R-Fork} creates a new \emph{child} thread, 
and \textsf{R-New} creates a new channel and binds its endpoints in 
a restriction. Rules \textsf{R-Com}, \text{R-Ch} and \textsf{R-Close} 
match, respectively, send and receive, select and match, 
close and wait operations in parallel threads. Configuration reduction 
also includes the usual rules for parallel execution 
(\textsf{R-Par}), reduction under restriction (\textsf{R-Bind}) 
and reduction up to structural congruence (\textsf{R-Cong}).

\paragraph{Auxiliary Results}
We start by proving that structural congruence ($\structcong$, cf. \cref{fig:reduction}, bottom) is type preserving (\Cref{t:cong}).
To this end, we require the following auxiliary results. 



\begin{lemma}[Strengthening]\
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item If $\istype{\envpoly, \tvar :: \pr}{\envpr}{T}$ and $\tvar\not\in\ftv{T}$ then $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr}{T}$.
    \item If $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars, x:T}{\envpr}{e}{U}{\pr}$
    and $x \not\in \fv{e}$, then $\lowestpriorityEnv{T} =_{\envpr} \prtop$
    and $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{e}{U}{\pr}$.
    \item If $\runtimetyping{\envtvars, x: T}{\config{C}}{\thread}$ and $x \not\in \fv{\config{C}}$
    then $\lowestpriorityEnv{T} =_{\envpr} \prtop$ and $\runtimetyping{\envtvars}{\config{C}}{\thread}$.
  \end{enumerate}  
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
  By rule induction on the first hypotheses.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}
  If $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr}{S}$ then $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr}{\dualof{S}}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
  By induction on the derivation $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr}{S}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Agreement for process formation]\
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item If $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{e}{T}{\pr}$
    then $\wfpolyctx{\envpoly}{\envpr}{\envtvars}$ and $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr}{T}$.
    \item If $\runtimetyping{\envtvars}{\config{C}}{\thread}$ then $\wfpolyctx{\emptyenv}{\emptyenv}{\envtvars}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  \begin{proof}\
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item By induction on the derivation of $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{e}{T}{\pr}$.
    \item By induction on the derivation of $\runtimetyping{\envtvars}{\config{C}}{\thread}$ using item 1. \qedhere
    \end{enumerate}
  \end{proof}
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Weakening]\
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item If $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr}{T}$ then $\istype{\envpoly, \tvar :: \pr}{\envpr}{T}$.
    \item If $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr}{T}$ then $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr, \prvar\in \intervalvar}{T}$.
    \item If $\wfpolyctx{\envpoly}{\envpr}{\envtvars}$ then $\wfpolyctx{\envpoly, \tvar :: \pr}{\envpr}{\envtvars}$.
    \item If $\wfpolyctx{\envpoly}{\envpr}{\envtvars}$ then $\wfpolyctx{\envpoly}{\envpr, \prvar \in \intervalvar}{\envtvars}$.
    \item If $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpoly}{e}{T}{\pr}$ then 
    $\typingpoly{\envpoly, \tvar :: \pr}{\envtvars}{\envpoly}{e}{T}{\pr}$.
    \item If $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpoly}{e}{T}{\pr}$ and 
    $\lowestpriorityEnv{U} =_{\envpr} \prtop$ then 
    $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars, x:U}{\envpoly}{e}{T}{\pr}$.
    \item If $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpoly}{e}{T}{\pr}$ then
    $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpoly, \prvar\in \intervalvar}{e}{T}{\pr}$.
    \item If $\runtimetyping{\envtvars}{\config{C}}{\thread}$ and $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr}{T}$
    and $\lowestpriorityEnv{T} =_{\envpr} \prtop$ then $\runtimetyping{\envtvars, x:T}{\config{C}}{\thread}$.
  \end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
  By induction on the first hypothesis, for each item.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Type Preservation}
We start by 
showing that values produce no effect and the priority of the context coincides with priority of their type.

\begin{lemma}
  \label{lem:values}
  If $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{v}{T}{\pr}$ then
  $\pr = \prbot$ and $\lowestpriorityEnv{\envtvars} =_{\envpr} \lowestpriorityEnv{T}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
   By induction on the derivation of $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{v}{T}{\pr}$.
\end{proof}

The next lemma is adapted from Almeida et 
al.~\cite{DBLP:journals/iandc/AlmeidaMTV22} and is used to prove
type preservation for communication reductions.

\begin{lemma}
  \label{lem:move-values}
  Let $\ctxsplit{\envpoly}{\envpr}{\envtvars}{\envtvars_1}{\envtvars_2}$ and 
  $\pr = \prglb{\pr_1}{\pr_2}$. We have 
  $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{\evalapp{\evalctx}{\e}}{T}{\pr}$
  if and only if 
  $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars_1}{\envpr}{e}{U}{\pr_1}$
  and 
  $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars_2, x:U}{\envpr}{\evalapp{\evalctx}{x}}{T}{\pr_2}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
  By rule induction on the structure of the evaluation context $E$, in both directions.
\end{proof}

The usual substitution lemmas now consider also priority substitution.

\begin{lemma}[Value substitution]
  If $\ctxsplit{\envpoly}{\envpr}{\envtvars}{\envtvars_1}{\envtvars_2}$ and
  $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars_1, x: U}{\envpr}{e}{T}{\pr_1}$
  and $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars_2}{\envpr}{v}{U}{\pr_2}$
  then $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{\subs{e}{v}{x}}{T}{\pr_1}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
    By induction on the derivation of $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars_1, x: U}{\envpr}{e}{T}{\pr_1}$,
    using~\cref{lem:values}.
 \end{proof}

 \begin{lemma}[Type substitution]\
  \label{lem:type-subst}
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item Suppose that $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr}{U}$. If 
    $\istype{\envpoly, \tvar::\pr}{\envpr}{T}$ 
    and $\lowestpriorityEnv{U} =_{\envpr} \pr$
    then 
    $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr}{\subs{T}{U}{\tvar}}$.
    \item If $\ctxsplit{\envpoly, \tvar::\pr}{\envpr}{\envtvars}{\envtvars_1}{\envtvars_2}$
    and $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr}{U}$
    and $\lowestpriorityEnv{U} =_{\envpr} \pr$
    then $\ctxsplit{\envpoly}{\envpr}{\subs{\envtvars}{U}{\tvar}}{\subs{\envtvars_1}{U}{\tvar}}{\subs{\envtvars_2}{U}{\tvar}}$
    \item If $\typingpoly{\envpoly, \tvar :: \pr}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{e}{T}{\pr_1}$
    and $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr}{U}$
    and $\lowestpriorityEnv{U} =_{\envpr} \pr$
    then $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\subs{\envtvars}{U}{\tvar}}{\envpr}{\etapp{e}{U}}{\subs{T}{U}{\tvar}}{\pr_1}$.
  \end{enumerate}
 \end{lemma}
 \begin{proof}\
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item By induction on the derivation of $\istype{\envpoly, \tvar::\pr}{\envpr}{T}$.
    \item By induction on the derivation of $\ctxsplit{\envpoly, \tvar::\pr}{\envpr}{\envtvars}{\envtvars_1}{\envtvars_2}$.
    \item By induction on the derivation of $\typingpoly{\envpoly, \tvar :: \pr}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{e}{T}{\pr_1}$, 
    using items 1 and 2.\qedhere
  \end{enumerate}
 \end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Priority substitution]\
  \label{lem:priority-subst}
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item If $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr, \prvar\in\intervalvar}{T}$
    and $\pr \in_\envpr \intervalvar$
    then $\istype{\subs{\envpoly}{\pr}{\prvar}}{\subs{\envpr}{\pr}{\prvar}}{\subs{T}{\pr}{\prvar}}$.
    \item If $\ctxsplit{\envpoly}{\envpr, \prvar\in\intervalvar}{\envtvars}{\envtvars_1}{\envtvars_2}$
    and $\pr \in_\envpr \intervalvar$ then
    $\ctxsplit{\subs{\envpoly}{\pr}{\prvar}}{\subs{\envpr}{\pr}{\prvar}}{\subs{\envtvars}{\pr}{\prvar}}{\subs{\envtvars_1}{\pr}{\prvar}}{\subs{\envtvars_2}{\pr}{\prvar}}$.
    \item If $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr, \prvar\in \intervalvar}{e}{T}{\pr_1}$
    and $\pr\in_\envpr \intervalvar$

  \end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}\
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item By induction on the derivation of $\istype{\envpoly}{\envpr, \prvar\in\intervalvar}{T}$.
    \item By induction on the derivation of $\ctxsplit{\envpoly}{\envpr, \prvar\in\intervalvar}{\envtvars}{\envtvars_1}{\envtvars_2}$.
    \item By induction on the derivation of $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr, \prvar\in \intervalvar}{e}{T}{\pr_1}$
    using items 1 and 2.\qedhere
  \end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Expression reduction is type preserving]
  If $\red{e_1}{e_2}$ and $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{e_1}{T}{\pr}$
  then $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{e_2}{T}{\pr}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
    By induction on the derivation of $\red{e_1}{e_2}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Configuration reduction is type preserving]
  \label{lem:subject-red-processes}
  If $\red{\config{C}_1}{\config{C}_2}$ and $\runtimetyping{\envtvars}{\config{C}_1}{\thread}$
  then $\runtimetyping{\envtvars}{\config{C}_2}{\thread}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
    By induction on the derivation of $\red{\config{C}_1}{\config{C}_2}$; for communication reductions use~\cref{lem:move-values}. 
\end{proof}

\subsection{Progress and deadlock-freedom}
We now focus on our ultimate goal of proving that well-typed 
(closed) configurations are guaranteed to be deadlock-free.

To facilitate the presentation, we 
introduce a few concepts, a\-dapt\-ed from the work by Kokke and Dardha~\cite{DBLP:journals/lmcs/KokkeD23}, that will allow us to describe the state of 
communication in a given expression.  
We say that an expression \emph{acts on a channel $x$} if it is 
of the form 
\begin{itemize}
	\item 
$\eapp{\eapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\esend}{\pr}}{T}}{\priority{\sigma}}}{S}}{v}}{x}$, or  $\eapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\ereceive}{\pr}}{T}}{\priority{\sigma}}}{S}}{x}$, 
\item $\eapp{\eprapp{\eclose}{\pr}}{x}$, or  $\eapp{\eprapp{\ewait}{\pr}}{x}$.
\end{itemize}
In this case, the expression is said to be an \emph{action}.
%

%   A term \emph{acts on a channel $x$} if it is of the form 
%   $\eapp{\eapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\esend}{\pr}}{T}}{\priority{\sigma}}}{S}}{v}}{x}$,
%   $\eapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\ereceive}{\pr}}{T}}{\priority{\sigma}}}{S}}{x}$, 
%   $\eapp{\eprapp{\eclose}{\pr}}{x}$, or 
%   $\eapp{\eprapp{\ewait}{\pr}}{x}$.
%   In this case, the term is said to be an \emph{action}.
% \end{definition}

%   where $\e_2$ is of the form $\enew{S}$ or $\eapp{\eprapp{\eprapp{\efork}{\pr}}{\prsigma}}{\e_3}$ or

Actions need to be extended to a notion that considers the 
other forms of \emph{readiness} to communicate.
We thus define an expression  $\e_1$ as \emph{ready} if it 
is of the form $\evalapp{\evalctx}{\e_2}$,
where $\e_2$ is of the form $\enew{S}$ or 
$\eapp{\eprapp{\eprapp{\efork}{\pr}}{\prsigma}}{\e_3}$ or 
$\e_2$ acts on channel $x$. In the latter case, 
$\e_1$ is said to be \emph{ready to act on $x$}.
%or \emph{is blocked on $x$}.

We now prove progress for the term language.

\begin{theorem}
  \label{thm:progress}
  If $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{\e}{T}{\pr}$ and
  for all $x: T\in \envtvars$, $T$ is a session type, then:
 (i)~$\e$ is a value, or
    (ii)~$\red{\e}{\e'}$ for some $\e'$, or
    (iii)~$\e$ is ready.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
  By rule induction on the hypothesis $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{\e}{T}{\pr}$.
    
    \emph{Cases T-Var, T-Const, T-TAbs, T-PAbs, T-Abs, T-Sel.}
    Variables, constants, term, type and priority abstractions, as well as $\eselect{k}$
    are all values.

    \emph{Case T-App.}
    In this case, $\e = \eapp{e_1}{e_2}$, $\Gamma = \Gamma_1\circ \Gamma_2$ and $\pr = \prglb{\pr_1}{\pr_2}$. 
    Premises to the rule include
    $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars_1}{\envpr}{e_1}{\tarrow{T_1}{T_2}{\pr}{\prsigma}{m}}{\pr_1}$
    and 
    $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars_2}{\envpr}{e_2}{T_1}{\pr_2}$.
    Since $\envtvars$ only has session types, $\envtvars_1$ and $\envtvars_2$ also only have sessions.
    By induction hypothesis on $e_1$, we can have three cases:\\
    \textbf{Case: $e_1$ is a value $v_1$.} In this case, we proceed by induction on $e_2$ and 
      we get three subcases:
      \begin{itemize}
        \item $e_2$ is a value $v_2$. Since $v_1$ has type $\tarrow{T_1}{T_2}{\pr}{\prsigma}{m}$, either:
        $v_1 = \eabs{x}{U}{e}{m}$, in which case $e$ reduces by \textsf{E-App}, or\\
        $v_1 = \eselect{k}$, which yields $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars_2}{\envpr}{v_2}{\tintchoice{\ell}{S_\ell}{L}{\pr'}}{\pr_2}$
          and so, by inversion on the typing rules, $v_2 = x$ and $e$ is ready, or\\
        $v_1 = \etapp{\eprapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\esend}{\pr}}{T}}{\prsigma}}{S}$, in which case 
          $\eapp{v_1}{v_2}$ is a value, or \\
        $v_1 = \eapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\esend}{\pr}}{T}}{\prsigma}}{S}}{v}$: similarly to  
          $\eselect{k}$, by inversion we should have $v_2 = x$ and so $e$ is ready, or\\
        $v_1 = \etapp{\eprapp{\etapp{\eprapp{\ereceive}{\pr}}{T}}{\prsigma}}{S}, 
          \eprapp{\eclose}{\pr'}, \eprapp{\ewait}{\pr'}$, were it is similar, or\\
        $v_1 = \eprapp{\eprapp{\efork}{\pr'}}{\pr''}$, in which case $\eapp{v_1}{v_2}$ is ready.
        \item $e_2$ reduces. Take $E = \eapp{v_1}{\evalhole{}}$ and $e$ reduces by \textsf{E-Ctx}.
        \item $e_2$ is ready and has the form $\evalapp{E}{e_2'}$. Take $E'=\eapp{v_1}{E}$
        and conclude that $e$ is ready.
      \end{itemize}
      \textbf{Case: $e_1$ reduces.} Take $E = \eapp{\evalhole{}}{e_2}$ and $e$ reduces by \textsf{E-Ctx}.\\
      \textbf{Case: $e_1$ is ready and has the form $\evalapp{E}{e_1'}$.} Take $E' = \eapp{E}{e_2}$ and 
      conclude that $e$ is ready.

    \emph{Cases T-TApp, T-PApp} are similar.

    \emph{Case T-Pair}. In this case, $e = \epair{e_1}{e_2}$. By induction hypothesis we 
    know that either both $e_1$ and $e_2$ are values, in which case $e$ is a value, 
    or one of them is not a value, say $e_1$. If $e_1$ reduces, consider the 
    context $E = \epair{\evalhole{}}{e_2}$ and conclude that $e$ reduces by \textsf{E-Ctx}. 
    If $e_1$ is ready and has the form $\evalapp{E}{e_1'}$, 
    consider the context $\epair{\evalapp{E}{e_1'}}{e_2}$ and conclude that $e$ is also ready.

    \emph{Case T-LetPair}. In this case $e = \eletpair{x_1}{x_2}{e_1}{e_2}$. By induction 
    hypothesis on $e_1$ we know that either: $e_1$ is a value, in which case $e_1 = \epair{v_1}{v_2}$
    and so $\e$ reduces by \textsf{E-PairElim}; or $e_1$ reduces, in which case we 
    consider $E = \eletpair{x_1}{x_2}{\evalhole{}}{e_2}$ to conclude that $e$ reduces;
    or $e_1$ is ready and has the form $\evalapp{E}{e_1'}$ we consider $E' = \eletpair{x_1}{x_2}{\evalapp{E}{e_1'}}{e_2}$ 
    and conclude that $e$ is ready.

    \emph{Cases T-LetUnit, T-Match} are similar.

    \emph{Case T-New}. In this case, $e = \enew{S}$. So, $e$ is ready by definition.
\end{proof}

Following the work by Kokke and Dardha, we introduce a
notion of canonical forms for configurations. We 
say that a configuration $\config{C}$ is in \emph{canonical form}
if it is of the form $\confnu{x_1}{y_1}{\ldots  \confnu{x_n}{y_n}{\confthread{\mainthread}{\e}}}$
or, when it has child threads, it is of the form 
\[\confnu{x_1}{y_1}{\ldots  \confnu{x_n}{y_n}{(\confpar{\confthread{\childthread}{e_1}}{\confpar{\ldots}{\confpar{\confthread{\childthread}{\e_m}}{\confthread{\mainthread}{\e}}}})}},\]
where no expression $\e_i$ is a value.

% \begin{definition}
%   A configuration $\config{C}$ is in \emph{canonical form}
%   if it is of the form $\confnu{x_1}{y_1}{... \confnu{x_n}{y_n}{\confthread{\mainthread}{\e}}}$
%   or, when it has child threads, is of the form 
%   $\confnu{x_1}{y_1}{... \confnu{x_n}{y_n}{(\confpar{\confthread{\childthread}{e_1}}{\confpar{...}{\confpar{\confthread{\childthread}{\e_m}}{\confthread{\mainthread}{\e}}}})}}$,
%   where no term $\e_i$ is a value.
% \end{definition}

\begin{lemma}
  \label{lem:congruent-to-canonical-form}
  If $\runtimetyping{\envtvars}{\config{C}}{\mainthread}$ then there exists some
  $\config{D}$ such that $\config{C}\structcong\config{D}$ and
  $\config{D}$ is in canonical form.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
  It follows from structural congruence, 
  observing that the only values that child threads might have 
  are of the form $\eunit$.
\end{proof}

% We say that $v$ is an \emph{unrestricted value} if 
% $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{v}{T}{\pr}$ 
% with $\lowestpriorityEnv{T} = \prtop$.

Intuitively, we say that a configuration   is \emph{deadlock-free} 
if either it reduces forever or, if it terminates, then
all child threads are able to reduce to unit and the main thread  
reduces to an unrestricted value. More precisely:

\begin{definition}
$\config{C}$ is \emph{deadlock-free} if 
$\config{C} \rightarrow^* \config{C}' \not \rightarrow$ then 
$\config{C}'\structcong \confthread{\mainthread}{v}$, where 
$v$ is such that $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{v}{T}{\pr}$ with $\lowestpriorityEnv{T} = \prtop$.
\end{definition}

We are finally able to prove deadlock freedom.

% \begin{definition}
%   A configuration $\config{C}$ is deadlock-free if 
%   $\config{C} \rightarrow^* \config{C}' \not \rightarrow$ and 
%   $\config{C}'\structcong \confthread{\mainthread}{v}$, where 
%   $v$ is an unrestricted value, i.e., $\typingpoly{\envpoly}{\envtvars}{\envpr}{v}{T}{\pr}$ with $\lowestpriorityEnv{T} = \prtop$.
% \end{definition}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{thm:canonical-forms-reduce}
  If $\runtimetyping{\emptyenv}{\config{C}}{\mainthread}$ and $\config{C}$ is in 
  canonical form, then $\red{\config{C}}{\config{D}}$ for some 
  $\config{D}$ or $\config{C}\structcong {\confthread{\mainthread}{v}}$, where $v$ is an unrestricted value.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
  Let $\config{C}$ be a configuration in canonical form. Assume that $\config{C}$ is of the form:
  \[\config{C}=\confnu{x_1}{y_1}{\ldots  \confnu{x_n}{y_n}{(\confpar{\confthread{\childthread}{e_1}}{\confpar{\ldots}{\confpar{\confthread{\childthread}{\e_m}}{\confthread{\mainthread}{\e}}}})}}.\]
  By \Cref{thm:progress}, we know that for each $e_i$, either:
  \begin{itemize}
    \item $\red{e_i}{e_i'}$, in which case we apply \textsf{R-LiftM}, \textsf{R-LiftC}
    and find $\config{D}$ such that $\red{\config{C}}{\config{D}}$, or
    \item $e_i$ is ready (provided that it cannot be a value by definition
    of canonical form).
  \end{itemize}
  Likewise, for $\e$, we either have a reduction $\red{\e}{\e'}$
  that is lifted to the configuration or, either, $\e$ is ready or it is a value.
  Assume \emph{all expressions} $\e_i$ are ready and pick the ready expression with 
  the smallest priority bound, $\e' \in\{e_1, \ldots, \e_m, \e\}$.\\
  \textbf{Case: $\e' = \evalapp{\evalctx}{\enew{S}}$.} We apply \textsf{R-New} and 
    then \textsf{R-LiftC}.\\
    \textbf{Case: $\e' = \evalapp{\evalctx}{\eapp{\eprapp{\eprapp{\efork}{\pr}}{\prsigma}}{\e_3}}$.} We apply \textsf{R-Fork} and then
    \textsf{R-LiftC}.\\
    \textbf{Case: $\e'$ is an action.} Then, it should be able to act on some
    endpoint $x: S$. Let $y:\dualof{S}$ be the dual endpoint of $x$. 
    Since channels are linear, there must be an expression $\e''\in \{\e_1,\ldots, \e_m, \e\}\setminus\{\e'\}$
    that uses $y$. The expression $\e''$ must either be ready or a value. We analyze these two cases:
    
      \textbf{Case: $\e''$ is ready.} 
      % By lemma~\ref{lem:priority-ready}, 
      % $\lowestpriorityEnv{\e'} = \lowestpriorityEnv{\e''} \neq\prtop, \prbot$.
      Expression $\e''$ must be ready to act on $y$, otherwise there would
      exist another action on $y$ with priority smaller than that of ${\e''}$,
      which contradicts our choice that $e'$ has lower priority.
      Hence, $e'$ and $e''$ reduce using \textsf{E-Com}, \textsf{E-CH} 
      or \textsf{R-Close}. Then, we apply \textsf{R-LiftC}.
      
      \textbf{Case: $\e''$ is a value.} Since $\config{C}$ is in canonical form, 
      $\e''$ can only be a value if $\e'' = \e$. Since $\e''$ is a value, it 
      is either $y$, $\epair{y}{v}$, $\epair{v}{y}$, or $\eabs{\_}{\_}{\e'''}{m}$, where $\e'''$
      contains $y$. In all these cases typing the expression in the main thread 
      would not lead to priority $\prtop$ (as is imposed by \textsf{C-Main}), 
      which leads to a contradiction.
      
  Suppose now that $\config{C} =\confnu{x_1}{y_1}{\ldots  \confnu{x_n}{y_n}{\confthread{\mainthread}{\e}}}$. By \Cref{thm:progress} we either have a reduction $e\rightarrow e'$, or $e$ is ready, or $e$ is a value. By the reasoning above, if $e$ is ready then it cannot be an action, otherwise we would need to have an endpoint in scope with the same (smallest) priority within the same expression, which is not possible; we are then left with \textsf{R-New} and \textsf{R-Fork} which where analyzed above. If $e$ is a value, by the reasoning above it cannot include endpoints and so $v$ is an unrestricted value.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
  If $\runtimetyping{\emptyenv}{\config{C}}{\mainthread}$, then $\config{C}$
  is deadlock-free.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
  By \Cref{lem:congruent-to-canonical-form}, there exists $\config{D}_1$
  in canonical form 
  such that $\config{C}\structcong\config{D}_1$. 
  We have that either $\config{D}_1$ reduces forever, in which case $\config{C}$ is deadlock-free, or
  we apply \Cref{thm:canonical-forms-reduce}, followed
  by \Cref{lem:subject-red-processes,lem:congruent-to-canonical-form}
  to get $\config{D}_1\rightarrow^*{\config{D}_n}$, where 
  $\runtimetyping{\emptyenv}{\config{D}_n}{\mainthread}$ and $\config{D}_n \not \rightarrow$.
  To show that $\config{D}_n \structcong \confthread{\mainthread}{v}$, we 
  first prove that $\config{D}_n$ does not contain any session type in scope. 
  
  For that purpose, let us assume that 
  $\config{D}_n = \confnu{x}{y}{\config{D}_{n+1}}$.
  By \textsf{C-New} we get $\runtimetyping{x:S, y:\dualof{S}}{\config{D}_{n+1}}{\mainthread}$.
  That is, $x$ and $y$ occur in $\config{D}_{n+1}$ and have
  compatible types. Thus, one of the following reductions should hold on
  $\config{D}_n$:
  \textsf{R-Com}, \textsf{R-Ch} or \textsf{R-Close}. This contradicts our
  hypothesis that $\config{D}_n \not \rightarrow$, so this case does not hold.
  
  This means that $\config{D}_n$ does not have any restrictions. Since it is 
  well-typed under the $\emptyenv$ context, $\config{D}_n$
  should be closed. Then, it must be structurally congruent to 
  $\confthread{\mainthread}{v}$, where $v$ is an unrestricted value. 
  We conclude that $\config{C}$ is deadlock-free.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Priorities in action}
We now revisit the example from \Cref{subsec:shift-mismatch}
to show that it is well-formed. 
The complete program should include 
a \lstinline|main| function, as well as functions \lstinline|server| and \lstinline|client|, which send and receive integer values:

\begin{lstlisting}
-- replicate here code from Sec. 2.4
server: ~forallp p belongsTo (bot,top) =>~ dualof InputStream ->~[top,p+1]~ ()
server x =                     
   let x = send 2 x~{p}~ in      
   server~{p+1}~ x           

client: ~forallp p belongsTo (bot,top) =>~ InputStream ->~[top,p+2]~ ()
client y =                     
   let (v, y) = receive y~{p}~ in 
   client~{p+1}~ y

main : ()
main = 
  let (r1,w1) = new InputStream in     
  let (r2,w2) = new InputStream in      
  fork~{top}{1}~ (\_:() 1-> server~{1}~ w1);     
  fork~{top}{2}~ (\_:() 1-> client~{2}~ r2);     
  filterStream~{1}{2}~ (\x: Int -> x == 2) r1 w2
\end{lstlisting}

The typing derivation starts by applying \textsf{T-LetPair} and \textsf{T-New}
twice to put \lstinline|r1|, \lstinline|w1|, 
\lstinline|r2|, \lstinline|w2| in the context. Then, it isolates the
first \lstinline|fork| using \textsf{T-LetUnit}. 
To check the typing of the first \lstinline|fork|, we apply \textsf{T-App} to split
the typing of constant \lstinline|fork| from the typing of the 
thunk \lstinline|\_:() 1-> server~{1}~ w1|. 
The typing of  \lstinline|fork| succeeds after applying \textsf{T-PApp}
twice, to abstract over the priorities---while checking that 
the priority instantiation \lstinline|~top~| belongs to the 
priority interval $\intervaloc{\prbot}{\prtop}$ and \lstinline|~1~| 
belongs to $\intervalcc{\prbot}{\prtop}$, as prescribed in the 
typing of \lstinline|fork| (\cref{fig:types-constants}). 
For   \lstinline|\_:() 1-> server~{1}~ w1|, we 
apply \textsf{T-Abs}, followed by \textsf{T-App} and are left with 
checking the well-formedness of   \lstinline|w1| and 
function \lstinline|server| against the types provided
in the program. For the second \lstinline|fork| the reasoning is similar.

To check the rest of the program, we 
apply \textsf{T-App} thrice, to 
account for each argument of \lstinline|filterStream~{1}{2}~|.
We apply \textsf{T-Var} to the arguments \lstinline|r1| and \lstinline|w2|. Although we have not detailed typing rules for integers, booleans 
and conditionals (for the sake of simplicity), we can easily adapt 
the standard rules (e.g.,~\cite{DBLP:books/daglib/0005958}) to check the 
well-formedness  of the first argument (\lstinline|\x: Int -> x == 2|).
Finally, we use \textsf{T-PApp} twice to check that 
\lstinline|filterStream~{1}{2}~| conforms to the provided type.

We would like to point out a small detail about notation. According to our proposal, the primitive \lstinline|new| is invoked over a session type (cf. Rule \textsf{T-New} in~\cref{fig:typing-rules-expr}). In contrast, in the current syntax of FreeST, \lstinline|new| expects a type application followed by application to unit (see the \lstinline|main| function presented in~\cref{subsec:ex1}). This minor discrepancy is due to our choice of not having \lstinline|new| as a constant, as discussed in~\cref{sec:semantics}, and is in line with former proposals of term languages for context-free session types~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/ThiemannV16,DBLP:journals/iandc/AlmeidaMTV22}.

% Note that using rule \textsf{T-New} instead of a constant for $\enew$, as discussed in~\cref{sec:semantics}, results in the notation for invoking the \lstinline|new| primitive to deviate slightly from the current FreeST syntax---as used in function \lstinline|main| in~\cref{subsec:ex1}.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related-work}
Closely related work has been discussed throughout the paper; here we provide a broader context by commenting on other works. 
\paragraph{Session Types}
Session types were proposed by Honda et al.~\cite{DBLP:conf/esop/HondaVK98,DBLP:conf/concur/Honda93} 
as a way of structuring communication in heterogeneously typed channels. The 
original theory of session types has been extended in many ways, including 
incorporating bounded polymorphism~\cite{Gay2008895,DARDHA2017253}, label 
dependency~\cite{10.1145/3371135} and types with non-regular recursion via 
con\-text-free session types~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/ThiemannV16}. 

Our work 
capitalizes on developments for context-free session types, 
including extensions with higher-order types~\cite{Costa2022}, impredicative polymorphism~\cite{DBLP:journals/iandc/AlmeidaMTV22},  
higher-order polymorphism~\cite{10.1007/978-3-031-30044-8_15}, algorithms for type equivalence~\cite{DBLP:conf/tacas/AlmeidaMV20}, subtyping~\cite{DBLP:conf/concur/SilvaMV23} and kind inference~\cite{Almeida_2023,jlamp}. These 
developments have been integrated in the compiler of the FreeST programming language~\cite{freest}. 
This line of work has focused on increasing the expressiveness of types,  adopting the view that programmers should have the liberty of writing typable programs with deadlocked behaviors.
Our work shows that aiming at expressivity does not really conflict with strong, type-based correctness guarantees, as context-free session types can be effectively extended with deadlock-freedom guarantees while still supporting programs not expressible in standard session types. 
%Despite focusing on significantly increasing the expressiveness of types, these developments have sacrificed fundamental guarantees of type safety, namely the guarantee of deadlock freedom. In this  work, we endow context-free session types with a mechanism to ensure the  absence of deadlocks. 

\paragraph{Type Systems for Deadlock Freedom}
The priority-based ap\-proach that we have incorporated on context-free session types can be traced back to seminal  work by Kobayashi~\cite{DBLP:conf/unu/Kobayashi02,DBLP:conf/concur/Kobayashi06}, who developed several type systems based on priorities for statically enforcing (dead)lock freedom for $\pi$-calculus processes, under linear type systems with \emph{usages}. The resulting classes of concurrent processes are deadlock-free by typing, and rather expressive: they can express process networks in cyclic topologies and encode typed $\lambda$-calculi and the sequencing behavior distinctive of session types~\cite{DBLP:conf/unu/Kobayashi02,DARDHA2017253}. 
%pioneered an approach that consists of a prioritization mechanism to guarantee deadlock-freedom--- also considering cyclic topologies. Our work arises from a  fusion between work on context-free session types and work that capitalizes on  priorities to ensure the absence of deadlocks.


Caires and Pfenning~\cite{DBLP:conf/concur/CairesP10} established 
a Curry-Howard correspondence between session types and intuitionistic linear logic, from which correctness guarantees such as 
deadlock freedom and confluence follow from proof-theoretical principles. 
Wadler~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/Wadler12} transferred this connection  to the classical setting. 
This Curry-Howard approach to session types enabled a number of extensions, including forms of 
typed observational equivalence~\cite{DBLP:journals/iandc/PerezCPT14} 
and dependent types~\cite{10.1145/2003476.2003499} as
well as integrations of processes, functions, and sessions~\cite{DBLP:conf/esop/ToninhoCP13}, to name just a few.
Also in this line we find nested session types~\cite{10.1007/978-3-030-72019-3_7}, which were proved to strictly extend context-free session types.
An outstanding limitation of the logic-based approach to session types is its support for  tree-like topologies only, which leaves out many real-world scenarios~\cite{DBLP:journals/jlap/DardhaP22}. 
Extensions of the logic-based approach with priorities, in order to support cyclic topologies, have been proposed in 
\cite{DBLP:conf/fossacs/DardhaG18} (for synchronous processes without recursive types) and in \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2110-00146,DBLP:journals/lmcs/0001024} (for asynchronous processes with recursive types). 

\paragraph{From Processes to Programs}
Strictly speaking, all previously mentioned works concern processes, not programs. 
Although processes are long known to encode concurrent programs, the difference is relevant, as the non-local analyses enabled by priorities can be more directly performed for processes (where communication constructs are explicit) than for programs (where communication arises via functional constructs, cf. \cref{fig:types-constants}). 
To our knowledge, Padovani and Novara were the first to adapt a type system for deadlock-freedom  for processes~\cite{padovani_linear_pi} to the case of higher-order concurrent programs~\cite{DBLP:conf/forte/PadovaniN15} (see also their   technical report~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364}); a source of inspiration for our developments, their work uses recursion and polymorphism, although in a limited way (see the discussion in~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364}). 
The example in \Cref{subsec:shift-mismatch} illustrates the expressiveness of our approach with respect to Padovani and Novara's.
Our work has been also influenced by the work of Kokke and Dardha~\cite{DBLP:journals/lmcs/KokkeD23}, who adapted Padovani and Novara's approach to the case of regular session types without recursion, which is subsumed by our work. 

% In recent years, there has been extensive research aimed at developing  concurrent programs  with deadlock-free guarantees~\cite{DBLP:conf/forte/PadovaniN15, DBLP:conf/fossacs/Padovani14}, also  involving session types~\cite{DBLP:journals/lmcs/KokkeD23,DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2110-00146, DBLP:journals/jlap/DardhaP22, DBLP:conf/fossacs/DardhaG18}.   More related to our proposal, Padovani began by proposing a deadlock-free system  for $\pi$-calculus and then proposed a mechanism to guarantee deadlock-freedom  for higher-order programs, using recursion and polymorphism, but in a limited  way (cf. concluding remarks of Padovani and  Novara~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364}).

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

In this work, we have extended context-free session types 
for high\-er-order concurrent programs~\cite{DBLP:conf/icfp/ThiemannV16,DBLP:conf/tacas/AlmeidaMV20} 
with 
priority-based mechanisms that  
deadlock freedom~\cite{padovani:hal-00954364,DBLP:journals/lmcs/KokkeD23,DBLP:conf/forte/PadovaniN15}. 
Our type system supports polymorphism and non-regular recursion, 
while providing strong correctness guarantees for communicating programs.

We find it remarkable that techniques for excluding deadlocks for linear types and regular session types can also be applied to the more expressive context-free session types. Intuitively, this can be interpreted as follows: deadlocks are a purely operational matter, tied to the underlying message-passing model, rather than to the (rich) type structures that govern communication behavior. Still, it is reassuring to confirm that priority-based approaches  scale to the expressive and developed setting of context-free sessions.  

Although foundational, our developments have a concrete practical dimension.
The design of our framework is aligned with FreeST, a programming 
language with context-free session types. 
Ongoing work concerns the incorporation of the type system presented here in FreeST's compiler. 
Currently, the implementation uses an SMT solver (Z3~\cite{de2008z3}) to decide the 
satisfiability of the priority restrictions collected during type checking. Finalizing and evaluating the implementation is part of future work.

title: Modeling Latent Partner Strategies for Adaptive Zero-Shot Human-Agent Collaboration
summary:
In collaborative tasks, being able to adapt to your teammates is a necessary
requirement for success. When teammates are heterogeneous, such as in
human-agent teams, agents need to be able to observe, recognize, and adapt to
their human partners in real time. This becomes particularly challenging in
tasks with time pressure and complex strategic spaces where the dynamics can
change rapidly. In this work, we introduce TALENTS, a strategy-conditioned
cooperator framework that learns to represent, categorize, and adapt to a range
of partner strategies, enabling ad-hoc teamwork. Our approach utilizes a
variational autoencoder to learn a latent strategy space from trajectory data.
This latent space represents the underlying strategies that agents employ.
Subsequently, the system identifies different types of strategy by clustering
the data. Finally, a cooperator agent is trained to generate partners for each
type of strategy, conditioned on these clusters. In order to adapt to
previously unseen partners, we leverage a fixed-share regret minimization
algorithm that infers and adjusts the estimated partner strategy dynamically.
We assess our approach in a customized version of the Overcooked environment,
posing a challenging cooperative cooking task that demands strong coordination
across a wide range of possible strategies. Using an online user study, we show
that our agent outperforms current baselines when working with unfamiliar human
partners.

title: The size of the sync basin resolved
summary:
Sparsely coupled Kuramoto oscillators offer a fertile playground for
exploring high-dimensional basins of attraction due to their simple yet
multistable dynamics. For $n$ identical Kuramoto oscillators on cycle graphs,
it is well known that the only attractors are twisted states, whose phases wind
around the circle with a constant gap between neighboring oscillators
($\theta_j = 2\pi q j/n$). It was conjectured in 2006 that basin sizes of these
twisted states scale as $e^{-kq^2}$ to the winding number $q$. Here, we provide
new numerical and analytical evidence supporting the conjecture and uncover the
dynamical mechanism behind the Gaussian scaling. The key idea is that, when
starting with a random initial condition, the winding number of the solution
stabilizes rapidly at $t \propto \log n$, before long-range correlation can
develop among oscillators. This timescale separation allows us to model the
winding number as a sum of weakly dependent variables, leading to a Central
Limit Theorem derivation of the basin scaling.

title: Six Decades Post-Discovery of Taylor's Power Law: From Ecological and Statistical Universality, Through Prime Number Distributions and Tipping-Point Signals, to Heterogeneity and Stability of Complex Networks
summary:
First discovered by L. R. Taylor (1961, Nature), Taylor's Power Law (TPL)
correlates the mean (M) population abundances and the corresponding variances
(V) across a set of insect populations using a power function (V=aM^b). TPL has
demonstrated its 'universality' across numerous fields of sciences, social
sciences, and humanities. This universality has inspired two main prongs of
exploration: one from mathematicians and statisticians, who might instinctively
respond with a convergence theorem similar to the central limit theorem of the
Gaussian distribution, and another from biologists, ecologists, physicists,
etc., who are more interested in potential underlying ecological or
organizational mechanisms. Over the past six decades, TPL studies have produced
a punctuated landscape with three relatively distinct periods (1960s-1980s;
1990s-2000s, and 2010s-2020s) across the two prongs of abstract and physical
worlds. Eight themes have been identified and reviewed on this landscape,
including population spatial aggregation and ecological mechanisms, TPL and
skewed statistical distributions, mathematical/statistical mechanisms of TPL,
sample vs. population TPL, population stability, synchrony, and early warning
signals for tipping points, TPL on complex networks, TPL in macrobiomes, and in
microbiomes. Three future research directions including fostering reciprocal
interactions between the two prongs, heterogeneity measuring, and exploration
in the context of evolution. The significance of TPL research includes
practically, population fluctuations captured by TPL are relevant for
agriculture, forestry, fishery, wildlife-conservation, epidemiology, tumor
heterogeneity, earthquakes, social inequality, stock illiquidity, financial
stability, tipping point events, etc.; theoretically, TPL is one form of power
laws, which are related to phase transitions, universality, scale-invariance,
etc.

title: A bibliometric study on mathematical oncology: interdisciplinarity, internationality, collaboration and trending topics
summary:
Mathematical oncology is an interdisciplinary research field where
mathematics meets cancer research. The field's intention to study cancer makes
it dynamic, as practicing researchers are incentivised to quickly adapt to both
technical and medical research advances. Determining the scope of mathematical
oncology is therefore not straightforward; however, it is important for
purposes related to funding allocation, education, scientific communication,
and community organisation. To address this issue, we here conduct a
bibliometric analysis of mathematical oncology. We compare our results to the
broader field of mathematical biology, and position our findings within
theoretical science of science frameworks.
  Based on article metadata and citation flows, our results provide evidence
that mathematical oncology has undergone a significant evolution since the
1960s marked by increased interactions with other disciplines, geographical
expansion, larger research teams, and greater diversity in studied topics. The
latter finding contributes to the greater discussion on which models different
research communities consider to be valuable in the era of big data and machine
learning. Further, the results presented in this study quantitatively motivate
that international collaboration networks should be supported to enable new
countries to enter and remain in the field, and that mathematical oncology
benefits both mathematics and the life sciences.

title: Transformers Beyond Order: A Chaos-Markov-Gaussian Framework for Short-Term Sentiment Forecasting of Any Financial OHLC timeseries Data
summary:
Short-term sentiment forecasting in financial markets (e.g., stocks, indices)
is challenging due to volatility, non-linearity, and noise in OHLC (Open, High,
Low, Close) data. This paper introduces a novel CMG (Chaos-Markov-Gaussian)
framework that integrates chaos theory, Markov property, and Gaussian processes
to improve prediction accuracy. Chaos theory captures nonlinear dynamics; the
Markov chain models regime shifts; Gaussian processes add probabilistic
reasoning. We enhance the framework with transformer-based deep learning models
to capture temporal patterns efficiently. The CMG Framework is designed for
fast, resource-efficient, and accurate forecasting of any financial
instrument's OHLC time series. Unlike traditional models that require heavy
infrastructure and instrument-specific tuning, CMG reduces overhead and
generalizes well. We evaluate the framework on market indices, forecasting
sentiment for the next trading day's first quarter. A comparative study against
statistical, ML, and DL baselines trained on the same dataset with no feature
engineering shows CMG consistently outperforms in accuracy and efficiency,
making it valuable for analysts and financial institutions.

title: Finding easy regions for short-read variant calling from pangenome data
summary:
Background: While benchmarks on short-read variant calling suggest low error
rate below 0.5%, they are only applicable to predefined confident regions. For
a human sample without such regions, the error rate could be 10 times higher.
Although multiple sets of easy regions have been identified to alleviate the
issue, they fail to consider non-reference samples or are biased towards
existing short-read data or aligners.
  Results: Here, using hundreds of high-quality human assemblies, we derived a
set of sample-agnostic easy regions where short-read variant calling reaches
high accuracy. These regions cover 87.9% of GRCh38, 92.7% of coding regions and
96.4% of ClinVar pathogenic variants. They achieve a good balance between
coverage and easiness and can be generated for other human assemblies or
species with multiple well assembled genomes.
  Conclusion: This resource provides a convient and powerful way to filter
spurious variant calls for clinical or research human samples.
